title: Building Forces — From Push to Kepler in One Artifact
concept_layer: forces change motion via F=ma; gravity, wind, drag, and attraction as additive vector fields; same equation, different worlds

capture_leaks.rigid_body: Mover treats each body as a point with mass. Rotation, internal structure, deformation — all deferred to later sequences.
capture_leaks.instantaneous_force_application: The model assumes forces apply continuously but Euler integration ticks discretely; small errors accumulate.
capture_leaks.closed_system: Energy should be conserved (minus drag), but numerical integration leaks energy; orbital stability requires corrections.
capture_leaks.deterministic_predictability: Three bodies is enough for chaos. The orbital mode with three movers hints; swarm + n-body push further.

limit: Forces are modeled as vectors that accumulate. This works for a falling ball and for a planet orbiting the sun because they share the same equation. What it cannot hold: deformable matter, quantum uncertainty, relativistic speeds, systems where the observer is entangled with the observed. This map is classical mechanics made touchable.

stages.title: From color to motion
stages.thinking: Color_Flashlight taught that color is not added to the world — it is revealed by choosing which wavelengths are offered. Now motion: not added to space, revealed by choosing which forces accumulate. Both hinge on what a source GIVES. The world then responds.
stages.code:
# Color_Flashlight:
#   light_color = chosen subset of wavelengths
#   surface response = filtering by material albedo
#
# Now:
#   force = chosen vector in R³
#   body response = F = m·a
#
# Both start with choosing what to offer.
# The world answers with what it does.

extends Node3D

# The foundational equation of classical mechanics:
#   F = m · a
#   a = F / m
#   v += a · Δt
#   p += v · Δt

stages.title: A body is (mass, position, velocity, acceleration)
stages.thinking: Before forces, define what is being pushed. Nature of Code calls it a Mover. Four fields. Mass is scalar (how heavy). Position is Vector3 (where). Velocity is Vector3 (how fast, which way). Acceleration is the buffer where forces accumulate before being applied. The whole physics of this map reduces to these four.
stages.code:
class Mover:
	var mass: float = 1.0
	var position_v: Vector3 = Vector3.ZERO
	var velocity: Vector3 = Vector3.ZERO
	var acceleration: Vector3 = Vector3.ZERO
	var bounce_damping: float = 0.5

# Configure several at once
const MOVER_CONFIGS := [
	{ "mass": 0.6, "pos": Vector3(-0.25, 0.35, 0.0), "vel": Vector3.ZERO },
	{ "mass": 1.0, "pos": Vector3(-0.08, 0.35, -0.1), "vel": Vector3.ZERO },
	{ "mass": 1.8, "pos": Vector3(0.12, 0.35, 0.05), "vel": Vector3.ZERO },
	{ "mass": 2.5, "pos": Vector3(0.28, 0.35, -0.05), "vel": Vector3.ZERO },
]
# Different masses, same forces — see different responses

stages.title: Forces accumulate, then apply
stages.thinking: apply_force(force) is not 'move this body.' It is 'add this to the acceleration buffer, divided by mass.' Many forces in one frame. At the end of the frame, acceleration becomes velocity becomes position. Then acceleration resets. This separation — accumulate, integrate, reset — is the heart of rigid-body physics.
stages.code:
# On Mover (conceptually):
func apply_force(force: Vector3) -> void:
	acceleration += force / mass  # F = m·a  →  a += F/m

func update(delta: float) -> void:
	velocity += acceleration * delta
	position_v += velocity * delta
	acceleration = Vector3.ZERO  # reset after applying

# In _step_physics:
for mover in _movers:
	# Gravity (mass-dependent — heavier = stronger pull)
	var gravity = Vector3(0, -gravity_strength, 0) * mover.mass
	mover.apply_force(gravity)
	
	# Wind (mass-independent — uniform push)
	if wind_enabled:
		mover.apply_force(Vector3(wind_strength, 0, 0))
	
	# Air resistance (velocity-dependent drag)
	mover.apply_force(_compute_drag(mover))
	
	mover.update(delta)  # then integrate

stages.title: Drag opposes velocity, scales with v²
stages.thinking: Quadratic drag is where the physics stops being linear. The drag force points opposite to velocity (decelerating the body) and grows with the square of speed. Slow bodies barely feel it; fast bodies slow dramatically. This is why cars have terminal velocity, why rain doesn't accelerate indefinitely, why a paratrooper’s terminal velocity is ~200 km/h.
stages.code:
# F_drag = -½ · Cd · |v|² · v̂
#   Cd = drag coefficient (shape + medium)
#   |v| = speed (magnitude of velocity)
#   v̂ = unit vector in direction of motion
#   minus sign: opposes motion

func _compute_drag(mover: Mover) -> Vector3:
	var speed = mover.velocity.length()
	if speed < 0.001:
		return Vector3.ZERO
	var drag_mag = 0.5 * drag_coefficient * speed * speed
	return -mover.velocity.normalized() * drag_mag

stages.title: Switch to orbital — same math, different world
stages.thinking: A mode toggle. Same movers, same apply_force, same update loop. But now the force is Newton's law of gravitation: F = G·m₁·m₂/r², pointing from the body toward the central mass. One equation does terrestrial physics (ball falls down) AND celestial mechanics (planet orbits sun). The same F=ma that lets the mover fall through wind and drag also sends planets around the star. Universality is the lesson.
stages.code:
elif _mode == Mode.ORBITAL:
	# Gravitational attraction to central body
	var dir: Vector3 = -mover.position_v
	var dist: float = dir.length()
	dist = clamp(dist, 0.04, 1.0)
	dir = dir.normalized()
	var strength: float = (orbital_G * central_mass * mover.mass) / (dist * dist)
	mover.apply_force(dir * strength)
	
	# Light drag for stability (numerical integration is leaky)
	mover.apply_force(_compute_drag(mover) * 0.3)

# Newton's law:  F = G · M · m / r²
# Direction: toward the massive body (attractive)
# This SAME equation gives: apples falling, moons orbiting, 
# galaxies colliding. Scale invariance is not a coincidence.

stages.title: Draw the force field as arrows
stages.thinking: Forces are invisible. We make them visible by sampling space: at each point in a grid, compute what force would act on a unit mass there, draw an arrow. ImmediateMesh with PRIMITIVE_LINES renders dozens of arrows per frame. In forces mode: arrows point down-and-right (gravity + wind). In orbital mode: arrows point radially inward, with length varying by 1/r². The field IS the theory, made geometric.

stages.title: Kepler's law visible — equal areas in equal time
stages.thinking: In orbital mode, draw triangles from the central body to the mover's position at fixed intervals. Kepler's second law: the line from sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal time. Fast near periapsis, slow near apoapsis — the triangles compensate. This is not added as a teaching overlay. It is an emergent visualization: run physics, record positions at intervals, draw triangles. The law reveals itself.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: A forces artifact knows what it is. Not a physics engine — a classical-mechanics demonstrator. F=ma does terrestrial and celestial work with the same line of code because Newton's universality is real. Drag teaches terminal velocity. The orbital toggle teaches scale invariance. The field arrows make the invisible visible. Kepler sweeps confirm the invariant. What this artifact refuses: deformation, chaos beyond n=3, quantum uncertainty, relativistic speeds. Those are doors to later sequences.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: forces accumulate on Mover bodies via apply_force(); gravity, wind, drag, and attraction share F=ma
# desire: learner feels that the same equation that drops a ball orbits a planet — universality of classical mechanics
# critical_parameter: mode toggle — FORCES (terrestrial with wind+drag) vs ORBITAL (celestial with inverse-square)
# triggers: sliders adjust gravity/wind/drag; mover positions record trails; sweep triangles reveal Kepler's second law
# emerges: the force field as a sampled invisible object; terminal velocity from v² drag; scale invariance of F=ma
# needs: 3 force sliders [has]; 4 movers [has]; trail rendering [has]; force-field arrows [has]; Kepler sweep [has]
# relationships: builds on Trans_Rotation (vectors in 3D); bridges to softbodies (when bodies deform) and swarm (when movers couple)
# truth: F = m · a is the simplest equation that still describes the fall of an apple and the orbit of the moon
